key_points: PM E-DRIVE subsidy for electric 2-wheelers ended July 31, 2026, with subsidy reduced from 10,000 to 5,000 per vehicle between Apr-Jul 2025
Effective EV scooter acquisition cost will increase by approximately 5,000 rupees post-subsidy withdrawal
August 2026 electric 2W market share declined versus July, signaling demand moderation but seasonality also a factor
Electric 2W penetration already exceeds 10%, suggesting market transition to product-led growth rather than subsidy-dependent
Future FAME III support likely to shift focus towards 3W and other segments rather than 2W
OEM capacity expansion planned within existing facilities, resulting in lower incremental capex intensity during ICE-to-EV transition
Industry economics increasingly dependent on product quality, distribution, service networks, and battery cost reduction rather than government incentives
catalysts: FAME III policy announcement and composition
Battery cost trajectory and localization initiatives
OEM financing and exchange offer strategies
Electric 3W and commercial vehicle subsidy announcements
reports.summary: The July 31, 2026 termination of PM E-DRIVE subsidies for electric 2-wheelers represents a structural inflection point from subsidy-driven to product-led growth. While short-term demand moderation is expected, India's massive 2W market with sub-10% EV penetration, combined with OEMs' efficient capacity planning and declining battery costs, supports a long-term secular EV adoption narrative that transcends government incentives.
reports.connection_narrative: India's electric vehicle subsidy regime has undergone a fundamental reset in 2026, with the PM E-DRIVE program's discontinuation of electric 2-wheeler support marking the end of an artificial demand acceleration phase. This policy shift is structurally significant because the government is deliberately transitioning the EV ecosystem from incentive dependency toward market-based competition, signaling confidence that technology and economics have matured enough to support organic adoption. Simultaneously, discussions around FAME III suggest policymakers view the 2W segment as sufficiently penetrated at over 10 percent market share and want to redirect scarce subsidy resources toward less-developed segments like 3-wheelers and commercial vehicles, which remain critical for India's broader decarbonization goals. The 2-wheeler OEMs including Hero, Bajaj, TVS, and emerging pure-play EV manufacturers like Ather and Ampere face a near-term headwind as the effective cost of entry-level EV scooters rises by roughly 5,000 rupees following the removal of 5,000 rupee per-vehicle subsidies, which could suppress price-sensitive consumer demand in the critical August-September period. However, these companies benefit from a structural advantage that often gets overlooked: their capacity expansion plans are designed to occur within existing manufacturing facilities rather than requiring entirely new greenfield plants, meaning the incremental capital expenditure intensity during the ICE-to-EV drivetrain migration will be far lower than historical precedent. As subsidy tailwinds evaporate, competitive advantage will increasingly flow to OEMs with superior product quality, extensive distribution networks, reliable after-sales service infrastructure, and most critically, access to low-cost battery technology through either backward integration or strategic supplier relationships. The single most important catalyst to monitor is the timing and composition of FAME III announcements, particularly whether the government includes any residual support mechanisms for 2-wheelers or accelerates support for 3W and commercial segments. The key risk to monitor is the possibility that demand moderation proves more severe than consensus expectations if price-sensitive consumers defer purchases or trade down to lower-specification ICE vehicles, which could pressure OEM volumes and margins in the near term and force aggressive competitive pricing that erodes profitability before scale and battery costs provide natural support.

Portfolio of 46.5 msf across 29 Grade A office assets with 93% committed occupancy and geographically diversified presence across 6 cities

Attractive distribution yields: 6.2% (FY27E), 6.8% (FY28E), 7.3% (FY29E) with 8.7% DPU CAGR over FY26-29E
Portfolio composition resilient to AI disruption with 46% GCC exposure and 31% front-office portfolio featuring marquee MNC tenants
Low leverage with LTV of 18% provides financial flexibility for future acquisitions and growth
Pan-India office market showing strong recovery with net absorption of 57msf in CY25 and estimated 51-61msf annually through CY28E
catalysts: 1.2 msf new developments in Bengaluru commencing operations in FY27
Realization of 25% mark-to-market potential on lease renewals and exits

reports.summary: Knowledge Realty Trust is India's largest office REIT with a high-quality, geographically diversified portfolio of 46.5 msf across prime micromarkets in Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Bengaluru. Initiating BUY coverage with INR 130 target (16% upside) based on strong leasing tailwinds, mark-to-market potential, and improving occupancy metrics expected to drive 9% NOI CAGR through FY29E. The REIT offers attractive distribution yields rising to 7.3% by FY29E with an 8.7% DPU CAGR, complemented by an AI-resilient tenant mix dominated by GCCs and front-office operations.
reports.connection_narrative: The Indian office real estate market is experiencing a structural recovery driven by robust demand from Global Capability Centers and multinational corporations relocating back to physical offices post-pandemic. Pan-India net absorption has accelerated to 57 million square feet in calendar year 2025, with Grade A vacancy tightening to 13 percent as of June 2026, creating a favorable environment for high-quality institutional landlords. Simultaneously, the REIT sector in India has matured as a yield-generating investment vehicle, with mandatory 90 percent distribution requirements providing consistent cash returns to unitholders alongside capital appreciation from occupancy ramp-ups and rental escalations. Knowledge Realty Trust specifically benefits from its dominance in the three best-performing office markets—Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Bengaluru—where it controls prime micromarket assets with strong pre-leasing pipelines. The REIT's portfolio composition is exceptionally resilient to artificial intelligence disruption with 46 percent exposure to Global Capability Centers, which are centers of excellence handling complex, high-value work rather than traditional IT services vulnerable to automation. The company faces a near-term catalyst of economic occupancy rising from 87 percent in June 2026 to above 90 percent by March 2027 as large multinational tenants ramp up their physical footprints in a staggered manner, while simultaneously benefiting from a 25 percent mark-to-market potential on its in-place rent of 99 rupees per square foot per month. With 1.2 million square feet of new developments set to commence operations in Bengaluru during FY27 and only 1.3 million square feet of average portfolio expiries annually, KRT is positioned to capture meaningful leasing spreads, supported by management having already locked in 58 percent of FY27 expiries at a 25 percent spread. The most critical catalyst to monitor is whether occupancy crosses 90 percent by March 2027 while maintaining or exceeding the projected 25 percent mark-to-market spread on renewals, as any slowdown in corporate expansion or deterioration in market rents could impact the assumed 9 percent NOI CAGR.
